cases.label: Western Wollemi / Gospers Mountain fire edge, NSW (Black Summer 2019-20)
cases.lossPngEncoding: palette PNG; pixel palette index = loss year minus 2000; index 0 (no loss) is transparent; north-up, EPSG:4326, bounds map to the full image edges
cases.note: Hansen/UMD tree-cover loss 2019-2020 inside the NSW NPWS fire perimeters for the 2019-20 season (mainly the Gospers Mountain fire, with NPWS record dates 2019-10-25 to 2020-02-09 (UTC) and 479,514 ha in total). In this 640x540-pixel window (about 15 km square), 39.7% of the area shows 2019-2020 loss and 98.6% of those loss pixels fall inside the mapped fire perimeters (which cover 52.5% of the window): the loss follows the fire edge, as a wide, irregular patchwork across forested ridges and gullies. Black Summer attribution: the research does not say climate change caused each fire. van Oldenborgh et al. (2021, NHESS 21, 941-960) found fire-weather conditions had become more likely (a significant increase of at least 30% in climate models, and a large trend in the ERA5 reanalysis, driven mainly by hotter extremes), so the risk of such a fire season rose. Burnt eucalypt forest often resprouts, so fire loss can be temporary (general ecology, not measured here). Hansen loss is canopy loss and cannot say what caused it: the fire perimeter is what shows the cause.
cases.lossLegendNote: Colour: focus years (lossYears) use a cividis-like ramp; other years are shown in a dim blue. The legend lists only years present in the window.

cases.label: South-west Queensland (Mitchell grass / mulga country) land clearing
cases.lossPngEncoding: palette PNG; pixel palette index = loss year minus 2000; index 0 (no loss) is transparent; north-up, EPSG:4326, bounds map to the full image edges
cases.note: Hansen/UMD tree-cover loss 2004-2008 with Queensland SLATS woody-vegetation clearing polygons for the periods 2003-04 to 2007-08 (SLATS replacement-land-cover class: Pasture 685 polygons). In this 640x540-pixel window (about 15 km square) 17.2% of the area has 2004-2008 loss (2006 alone: 12.19%), and 93.5% of it falls inside SLATS clearing polygons. The loss comes as large rectangular blocks with straight edges, not a fire-shaped patchwork. SLATS records the replacement land cover as pasture, so this is land-use change by clearing, decided by people; it is not a climate effect. (Hansen years and SLATS reporting periods, which run roughly mid-year to mid-year, line up only approximately.)
